title: Problems: growing and judging one tree

items.prose: An exchange's surveillance team reviewed 60 alerts on large orders: 18 were spoofing and 42 were genuine. A tree's first question is *was more than 90% of the order cancelled?* Yes: 22 alerts, 14 spoofing and 8 genuine. No: 38 alerts, 4 spoofing and 34 genuine.

parts.question: Each side predicts its majority. How many of the 60 alerts does this one question get wrong?

feedback.correct: The yes side predicts spoofing and misses its 8 genuine alerts; the no side predicts genuine and misses 4 spoofs. That is 12.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. On each side, count the alerts outside the majority, then add.

byKey.parent: 18 is what the root alone gets wrong, calling every alert genuine. Count the minority on each side of the question.
byKey.majority: You counted the majorities, the alerts each side gets right. The mistakes are the minorities: 8 and 4.
byKey.one-side: 8 is the yes side's mistakes only. The no side also misses its 4 spoofs.

explain.text: Yes side: 14 spoofing against 8 genuine, so it says spoofing and gets 8 wrong. No side: 34 genuine against 4 spoofing, so it gets 4 wrong. The question cuts the root's 18 mistakes to 12.

parts.question: What is the Gini impurity of the root, all 60 alerts? Give an exact decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the two shares, square each, and subtract both squares from 1.

byKey.error-rate: 0.3 is the spoofing share, the root's error rate. Gini squares the shares: $1 - 0.3^2 - 0.7^2$.
byKey.sum-squares: 0.58 is $0.3^2 + 0.7^2$. Gini is 1 minus that sum.
byKey.no-two: 0.21 is $0.3 \times 0.7$. With two classes Gini is twice that, $2 \times 0.3 \times 0.7$.

parts.question: What is the weighted Gini of the two sides? Weight each side's Gini by its share of the 60 alerts. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Yes side $G = 0.463$ on 22 alerts, no side $G = 0.188$ on 38: $\tfrac{22}{60} \times 0.463 + \tfrac{38}{60} \times 0.188 = 0.289$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each side's Gini, weight it by its share of the 60 alerts, and add.

byKey.unweighted: You averaged the two sides equally. The no side holds 38 of the 60 alerts, so it weighs more.
byKey.yes-only: 0.463 is the yes side's Gini alone. Add the no side, and weight each by its share of the alerts.
byKey.gain: That is the gain, the drop from 0.42. The question asks for the impurity left after the split.

parts.question: Use the root's 0.42 and the sides' 0.289 from parts 2 and 3. What is the Gini gain of the question? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The gain is the root's impurity minus the weighted impurity of the sides.

byKey.child: 0.289 is what the split leaves. Take it from the root's 0.42.
byKey.carried: You subtracted the unweighted average, 0.326. Weight the sides by 22 and 38 alerts first: 0.289.
byKey.mistakes: That is the fall in the error rate, from 18 to 12 mistakes in 60. The question asks for the Gini gain.

explain.text: Gain $= 0.42 - 0.289 = 0.131$. The mistakes fell by 6 of 60, a drop of 0.1 in the error rate. Gini measures the purer mix too, not only the changed majorities.

parts.question: The yes side is split again by asking whether the order rested for under 2 seconds. One side gets 12 spoofing and 1 genuine. The other gets 2 spoofing and 7 genuine. The no side stays a leaf. How many of the 60 alerts does this depth-2 tree get wrong?

feedback.correct: The new leaves miss 1 and 2 alerts, and the no leaf still misses 4: $1 + 2 + 4 = 7$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the minority in each of the three leaves, then add.

byKey.no-leaf: 3 counts only the two new leaves. The no side is still a leaf, and it still misses 4 spoofs.
byKey.carried: 12 is the one-question tree from part 1. The second question fixes some of the yes side's 8 mistakes.
byKey.spoof-only: You counted only the spoofs that slip through, 2 and 4. The leaf of 12 spoofs also flags 1 genuine alert.

explain.text: Leaf 12 and 1 says spoofing and misses 1; leaf 2 and 7 says genuine and misses 2; the no leaf misses 4. The second question cut the mistakes from 12 to 7. Growing greedily, one best question at a time, is how the tree was built.

items.prose: A funding desk forecasts a repo's cost above the base rate, in bp, from its term. Six past trades: terms of 1, 2, 4, 6, 9 and 15 weeks, costs of 5, 7, 6, 13, 9 and 20 bp. A regression tree tries every midpoint between neighbouring terms.

parts.question: With no split, the tree forecasts one number for all six trades. What is the squared error of that forecast, summed over the six, in bp²?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Forecast the mean of the six costs, then add the squared gaps.

byKey.unsquared: You added the gaps without squaring them: $5 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 1 + 10$. Square each gap first.
byKey.mean-error: You divided by 6, which is the mean squared error. The question asks for the sum.
byKey.median: You forecast the median, 8. A regression leaf forecasts the mean, 10, which leaves less squared error.

explain.text: The best single forecast is the mean, $60/6 = 10$ bp. The squared gaps are 25, 9, 16, 9, 1 and 100. They add to 160.

parts.question: Using the root's 160 from part 1, which split removes the most squared error? Give that drop, in bp².

feedback.correct: The split at 12 weeks puts the 15-week trade alone. The left five have mean 8 and leave 40, so the drop is $160 - 40 = 120$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each midpoint, add the two sides' squared errors around their own means, and subtract from 160.

byKey.left-over: 40 is what the best split leaves. The drop is $160 - 40$.
byKey.even: 96 is the drop at 5 weeks, three trades each side. Splitting off the 20 bp trade at 12 weeks removes more.
byKey.first: 30 is the drop at 1.5 weeks, the first midpoint. Try them all: the one at 12 weeks removes 120.

explain.text: The drops at 1.5, 3, 5, 7.5 and 12 weeks are 30, 48, 96, 60.75 and 120. At 12 weeks the right leaf holds 20 alone and the left leaves $9 + 1 + 4 + 25 + 1 = 40$. So the tree splits at 12 weeks.

parts.question: Take the split at 12 weeks as a one-split tree. What does it forecast for a new 26-week repo, in bp?

feedback.correct: 26 weeks is above 12, so the repo lands in the right leaf. That leaf holds one trade, at 20 bp.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Answer the one question for 26 weeks, then read that leaf's mean.

byKey.root: 10 is the forecast with no split. The tree first asks whether the term is above 12 weeks.
byKey.left: 8 is the left leaf, for terms up to 12 weeks. 26 weeks goes right.
byKey.carried: 14 is the right leaf of the split at 5 weeks. The best split is at 12 weeks, whose right leaf holds only the 20 bp trade.

explain.text: Every term above 12 weeks lands in the right leaf, whose mean is 20 bp. The forecast is the same at 26 weeks as at 15. A tree cannot extend a trend past its last leaf.

parts.question: The desk refits with `min_samples_leaf=2`. Which split does the tree now choose? Give its drop in squared error, in bp².

feedback.correct: Each side needs 2 trades, so only 3, 5 and 7.5 weeks remain. At 5 weeks the sides leave 2 and 62, so the drop is $160 - 64 = 96$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the splits with at least 2 trades on each side, and take the largest drop.

byKey.no-floor: 120 needs a leaf of one trade. With `min_samples_leaf=2` the split at 12 weeks is not allowed.
byKey.left-over: 64 is what the split at 5 weeks leaves. The drop is $160 - 64$.
byKey.next-door: 60.75 is the drop at 7.5 weeks. The split at 5 weeks removes more, 96.

explain.text: The allowed drops are 48 at 3 weeks, 96 at 5 and 60.75 at 7.5. At 5 weeks the left leaf, 5, 7 and 6, has mean 6 and leaves 2; the right, 13, 9 and 20, has mean 14 and leaves 62. So the drop is 96.

parts.question: Use the split at 5 weeks from part 4. What does the floored tree forecast for the 26-week repo, in bp?

feedback.correct: 26 weeks is above 5, so it lands in the leaf of 13, 9 and 20 bp. Their mean is 14.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Answer the 5-week question for 26 weeks and read that leaf's mean.

byKey.carried: 20 is the unfloored tree, whose right leaf was one trade. With the floor the right leaf holds three.
byKey.left: 6 is the left leaf, for terms up to 5 weeks. 26 weeks goes right.
byKey.root: 10 is the mean of all six. The floored tree still asks one question first.

explain.text: The right leaf averages 13, 9 and 20 to 14 bp. The floor stops a forecast resting on one trade, so the long-term forecast falls from 20 to 14. Either way it is flat past the data.

items.prose: A broker's tree predicts which of 400 clients close their account within a year. One internal node holds 27 clients: 18 stayed and 9 left. It first splits off 7 clients who all left. The other 20, 18 stayed and 2 left, split again: 15 who stayed, and 5 of whom 3 stayed and 2 left.

parts.question: What is the Gini impurity of the node of 27 clients? Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the two shares, add them, and subtract from 1.

byKey.error-rate: $\tfrac{1}{3}$ is the share who left, the node's error rate. Gini squares the shares.
byKey.sum-squares: 0.5556 is the sum of the squared shares. Gini is 1 minus it.
byKey.no-two: 0.2222 is $\tfrac{2}{3} \times \tfrac{1}{3}$. With two classes Gini is twice that.

parts.question: Pruning scores a node by its Gini times its share of all 400 clients, $R(t)$. Using $G = \tfrac{4}{9}$ from part 1, what is $R(t)$ for this node? Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the node's Gini by 27 out of 400.

byKey.unweighted: 0.4444 is the Gini itself. $R(t)$ weights it by the node's share of the 400 clients.
byKey.carried: You weighted the error rate, $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Use the Gini, $\tfrac{4}{9}$.
byKey.carried-squares: You weighted the sum of the squared shares, $\tfrac{5}{9}$. Use the Gini, $1 - \tfrac{5}{9} = \tfrac{4}{9}$.

explain.text: The node holds $\tfrac{27}{400} = 0.0675$ of the clients. $R(t) = 0.0675 \times \tfrac{4}{9} = 0.0300$, the impurity it carries as one leaf.

parts.question: Look at the inner node of 20 clients, 18 stayed and 2 left. At what `ccp_alpha` does cutting it back to one leaf break even? Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: As one leaf: $\tfrac{20}{400} \times 0.18 = 0.009$. Its two leaves: $\tfrac{5}{400} \times 0.48 = 0.006$ and 0. The cut removes 1 leaf, so $\alpha = 0.009 - 0.006 = 0.0030$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $R$ for the node as one leaf and for its two leaves. Divide the difference by the leaves the cut removes.

byKey.no-subtract: 0.009 is $R$ for the node as one leaf. Subtract what its two leaves carry, 0.006.
byKey.halved: You divided by 2. Two leaves become one, so the cut removes 1 leaf.
byKey.leaf-only: 0.006 is what the two leaves carry. The break-even is the extra impurity of the cut, $0.009 - 0.006$.

explain.text: The node of 18 and 2 has $G = 0.18$, so $R = 0.05 \times 0.18 = 0.009$. Its leaves carry $0.0125 \times 0.48 = 0.006$, since the 15 who stayed form a pure leaf. Cutting costs 0.003 for 1 leaf, so $\alpha = 0.003$.

parts.question: Once that cut is made, the node of 27 has two leaves: the 7 who left, and the 20 with $R = 0.009$. Using $R(t) = 0.03$ from part 2, at what `ccp_alpha` does cutting the node of 27 to one leaf break even? Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The leaves carry $0.009 + 0 = 0.009$ and the cut removes 1 leaf: $\alpha = 0.03 - 0.009 = 0.0210$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract what the two leaves carry from 0.03, and divide by the one leaf the cut removes.

byKey.three-leaves: You scored the branch with all three of its first leaves, $(0.03 - 0.006)/2$. The inner node was cut first, so the node now has two leaves.
byKey.no-subtract: 0.03 is $R(t)$ itself. Subtract what the two leaves carry, 0.009.
byKey.halved: You divided by 2. The node now has two leaves, so the cut removes 1.

explain.text: The 7 who left form a pure leaf, so the leaves carry 0.009 in all. Cutting the node adds $0.03 - 0.009 = 0.021$ and removes 1 leaf. This is how pruning runs: cut the weakest link, then score the branches again.

parts.question: The full tree has 11 leaves, and every other cut on its pruning path is above 0.024. Using 0.003 and 0.021 from parts 3 and 4, how many leaves does `DecisionTreeClassifier(ccp_alpha=0.016)` keep?

feedback.correct: 0.003 is at most 0.016, so the inner node is cut and 1 leaf goes. 0.021 is above 0.016, so the node of 27 keeps its two leaves: 10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make every cut whose break-even is at most 0.016, then count the leaves left.

byKey.carried: You made both cuts, as a break-even of 0.012 would. The node of 27 breaks even at 0.021, above 0.016, so it stays split.
byKey.not-cut: The inner node breaks even at 0.003, below 0.016, so it is pruned.
byKey.three: You took away all three of the branch's leaves. Only the inner node is cut, and it loses 1 leaf.

explain.text: Pruning at 0.016 makes every cut on the path at or below 0.016: only the inner node's, at 0.003. So 11 leaves become 10. Choose `ccp_alpha` by cross-validation on the training clients, not on the test set.

items.prose: A desk labels ten mornings by whether the index rose after the open, using the opening gap in %. Down mornings had gaps of $-1.4$, $-0.9$, $-0.6$, $-0.2$, $0.5$ and $2.4$. Up mornings had gaps of $0.3$, $0.9$, $1.2$ and $1.7$. A tree scans every midpoint.

parts.question: How many candidate thresholds does the scan try on the gap?

feedback.correct: Ten distinct values have 9 spaces between neighbours, so 9 midpoints.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort the ten gaps and count the spaces between neighbours.

byKey.per-day: A threshold sits between two neighbouring values. Ten values in a row have 9 spaces between them.
byKey.boundaries: 4 counts only the places where the label changes. The scan tries every midpoint, 9 of them.

explain.text: Sorted, the gaps run $-1.4, -0.9, -0.6, -0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.9, 1.2, 1.7, 2.4$. A threshold goes halfway between each neighbouring pair, so there are 9.

parts.question: The splits at 0.05 and at 0.7 both leave 2 mistakes. What is the Gini gain of the split at 0.05? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The root has $G = 0.48$. Left of 0.05: 4 down, pure. Right: 2 down and 4 up, $G = \tfrac{4}{9}$. Gain $= 0.48 - 0.6 \times \tfrac{4}{9} = 0.213$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the root's Gini and each side's, weight the sides by 4 and 6 mornings, and subtract.

byKey.child: 0.267 is the Gini of the two sides, weighted by size. The gain is what the split took off the parent's 0.48.
byKey.unweighted: You gave both sides the same weight. The right side holds 6 of the 10 mornings.
byKey.other: 0.163 is the gain of the split at 0.7. This part asks for the split at 0.05.

explain.text: Root: 4 up of 10, $G = 1 - 0.16 - 0.36 = 0.48$. The left 4 mornings are pure; the right 6 have $G = 1 - \tfrac{1}{9} - \tfrac{4}{9} = 0.444$. Gain $= 0.48 - 0.6 \times \tfrac{4}{9} = 0.213$.

parts.question: What is the Gini gain of the split at 0.7? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Left of 0.7: 5 down and 1 up, $G = 0.278$. Right: 1 down and 3 up, $G = 0.375$. Gain $= 0.48 - (0.6 \times 0.278 + 0.4 \times 0.375) = 0.163$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the left side by 6 mornings and the right by 4, and subtract from 0.48.

byKey.child: 0.317 is the Gini of the two sides, weighted by size. Subtract it from 0.48.
byKey.unweighted: You gave both sides the same weight. Weight them by 6 and 4 mornings.
byKey.carried: 0.213 is the split at 0.05 from part 2. Score the split at 0.7 on its own sides.

parts.question: Using the gains 0.213 and 0.163 from parts 2 and 3, the tree keeps one of the two splits. What is its information gain with entropy, in bits? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The tree keeps 0.05, the larger Gini gain. The root's entropy is 0.971 bits and the right side's 0.918, so $0.971 - 0.6 \times 0.918 = 0.420$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the split with the larger Gini gain, then subtract its weighted child entropy from the root's.

byKey.other: 0.256 is the information gain of the split at 0.7. The tree keeps the split with the larger Gini gain, 0.05.
byKey.gini: 0.213 is the Gini gain. This part asks for the entropy version.
byKey.child: 0.551 is the entropy of the two sides, weighted by size. Take it from the root's 0.971.

explain.text: Root: $H(0.4) = -0.4\log_2 0.4 - 0.6\log_2 0.6 = 0.971$. The right 6 mornings have $H(\tfrac{1}{3}) = 0.918$ and the left 4 are pure. So the gain is $0.971 - 0.6 \times 0.918 = 0.420$ bits, and entropy prefers the same split.

parts.question: The desk grows the tree on the gap with no limit, until every leaf is pure. How many leaves does it end with?

feedback.correct: In order of gap the labels run in 5 unbroken runs: 4 down, 1 up, 1 down, 3 up, 1 down. Each run becomes one pure leaf.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort the mornings by gap and count the runs of one label.

byKey.per-day: A leaf holds every neighbouring morning with the same label, so a run of 4 downs is one leaf.
byKey.boundaries: 4 is the number of places where the label changes. The leaves sit between them, one more.
byKey.depth: 8 is $2^3$, a full tree of depth 3. This tree stops on each branch once it is pure.

explain.text: Every split falls where the label changes, so each pure leaf is one run of a label. There are 5 runs, so 5 leaves, and the tree is right on all ten mornings. The leaf at 0.5 holds a single morning: the tree has memorised it.
